question: How does one repeated bass note hold a long melody in place?
intro: A troubadour sings before a medieval castle, over a bass note that never leaves G♯. Listen to the song and to the drone beneath it. Instruments named here follow Ravel’s orchestration, the probable but undocumented version.

cues.title: Drone, bassoons, then the saxophone
cues.text: Bassoons play over a cello drone in 6/8 and G♯ minor; within twenty seconds an alto saxophone takes up the song, the troubadour’s voice. The bass pitch stays on G♯ in 53 of the 57 five-second windows: the song moves, the foundation does not.
cues.evidence: The bass pitch class reads A♭ (the same note as G♯) in 53 of the 57 windows of the report, including the first. Bassoons over a cello drone and the 6/8 metre: Philharmonia guide and the score (Mutopia, il-vecchio-castello.ly); alto saxophone for the theme: Philharmonia guide and Wikipedia. Boundary at 0:18 (novelty 0.78), consistent with the first statement settling; the report cannot time the entrance of an instrument.

cues.title: A watercolour of an Italian castle
cues.text: No picture called The Old Castle hung in the exhibition. Steinberg thinks it recalls one of Hartmann’s Italian architectural watercolours, and Stasov wrote of a castle with a troubadour before it. Hartmann often drew small figures beside his buildings for scale.
cues.evidence: Michael Steinberg’s Boston Symphony note (https://www.bso.org/works/pictures-at-an-exhibition) for the missing item and the Italian watercolours; Wikipedia’s article, section “The Old Castle”, for Hartmann’s habit of adding figures for scale. Related edge: hartmann-pictures--mussorgsky-pictures-1874. The note sits over the quietest window (−16.6 dB at 0:45).

cues.title: The sound thickens
cues.text: At about 1:40 the level climbs towards the first peak of the movement, at 1:45–1:50. The drone continues, but more instruments surround the tune; the strongest boundary of the report, at 1:58, closes this swell.
cues.evidence: Boundary at 1:40 (novelty 0.78); relative level −9.9 dB at 1:40 and −7.1 and −7.0 dB at 1:45 and 1:50; strongest boundary 1:58 (novelty 1.00). The thicker scoring is a listening interpretation from the level rise, not an identification of instruments.

cues.title: A premiere that sold out
cues.text: Boris Godunov reached the Mariinsky stage on 27 January 1874. Golenishchev-Kutuzov recalled nine sold-out performances that winter, but hostile reviews and the break-up of the Five left Mussorgsky isolated as he began his Hartmann memorial.
cues.evidence: Wikipedia’s Pictures at an Exhibition article (composition history), quoting Golenishchev-Kutuzov’s recollection of nine performances with the theatre sold out; the première date is in content/influence/romantic.json (edge pushkin-boris-godunov--mussorgsky-boris-1868). The note sits in a quieter stretch (−14 dB at 2:05–2:10).

cues.title: A long loud plateau
cues.text: From about 2:25 to 2:55 the level stays high, between −6 and −10 dB, with few new attacks. The tune is sustained rather than repeated in short figures; follow its long notes against the unchanged G♯ below.
cues.evidence: Relative level is −8.1, −6.2, −8.0, −9.3, −8.2, −7.8 dB at 2:25–2:50 with 0.0–0.6 onsets per second (except 1.4 at 2:40); loudest windows include 2:30. The drone is from the bass pitch class (G♯ in each of these windows).

cues.title: A modest orchestra, one new colour
cues.text: Steinberg notes that Ravel kept his orchestra about the size of Rimsky-Korsakov’s for Boris Godunov, then went beyond it with percussion and, most remarkably, the alto saxophone he gives this very picture. Ravel was not adding bulk; he was choosing a colour.
cues.evidence: Michael Steinberg’s Boston Symphony note (https://www.bso.org/works/pictures-at-an-exhibition) says Ravel made the orchestra the size of Rimsky-Korsakov’s Boris, added percussion and used the alto saxophone “most remarkably” in this movement. The note sits in the quiet stretch 3:00–3:12 (−15.9 to −14.9 dB).

cues.title: The strongest climax
cues.text: Around 3:15 the level jumps from −15.7 dB to −8.6 dB and reaches its maximum, −5.8 dB, at 3:20. This is the song at full strength; the drone still sits beneath it.
cues.evidence: Relative level is −15.7 dB at 3:10, −8.6 at 3:15 and −5.8 at 3:20, the loudest window of the movement; boundary at 3:14 (novelty 0.73). The bass pitch class remains A♭ (G♯) at 3:15–3:40.

cues.title: The life ebbs away
cues.text: After a last swell near 4:15 the level falls by about seven decibels at 4:20 and keeps softening. The bassoon takes up the drone, and the saxophone gives a last defiant cry before the end.
cues.evidence: Relative level is −6.9 dB at 4:15, −13.4 at 4:20 and −16.3 at 4:25 (boundary 4:24, novelty 0.57). The bassoon taking up the drone and the saxophone’s last cry: Philharmonia guide; the report cannot time them.

transitions.title: The drone stays; the sound thickens
transitions.how: Nothing changes in the bass: the G♯ drone runs on, so the join is heard as a change of weight, not of key. Around 1:40 the level rises towards its first peak at 1:45–1:50 and the accompaniment surrounding the tune thickens. A tonic pedal lets Mussorgsky repeat the song with changing colour and level while the harmony hardly moves.
transitions.evidence: Boundary at 1:40 (novelty 0.78); relative level −11.7 dB (1:35), −9.9 dB (1:40), −7.1 and −7.0 dB (1:45, 1:50); the bass pitch class is G♯ (A♭) in 53 of 57 windows. The pedal and 6/8 metre are in the piano score; the orchestral thickening is not identified by instrument.

transitions.title: A quiet gap, then the full song
transitions.how: After a hushed stretch at about −15 dB the sound surges at 3:14. The bass is still G♯, now under the loudest statement of the tune. The effect rests on contrast of level, not harmony: a tonic pedal under both the hush and the surge lets the same drone support the quietest and loudest music of the movement.
transitions.evidence: Relative level −15.9, −14.9 and −15.7 dB at 3:00, 3:05 and 3:10, then −8.6 (3:15) and −5.8 dB (3:20, the loudest window); boundary at 3:14 (novelty 0.73). Bass pitch class A♭ (G♯) from 3:15 to 3:40.

transitions.title: The song thins out and fades
transitions.how: A last swell near 4:15 gives way to a steady decline. The level drops by about seven decibels at 4:20; the bassoon takes up the drone and the saxophone makes a final, defiant entry. The movement ends without a loud cadence: the G♯ foundation is still present as the sound fades, so the close is a withdrawal of energy, not a change of harmony.
transitions.evidence: Relative level −6.9 dB (4:15), −13.4 dB (4:20), −16.3 dB (4:25) and −16.0 dB (4:40); boundary at 4:24 (novelty 0.57); bass pitch class A♭ (G♯) in the closing windows. Bassoon and saxophone roles: Philharmonia guide.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Skidmore College Orchestra (orchestra, as stated by the Free Music Archive; conductor unknown)
fields.note: The Commons page names no performer (“see Musopen for performance author information”). The Free Music Archive album of 15 tracks by the Skidmore College Orchestra lists a track of the same title and length (4:46; this file is 4:44), and the Internet Archive item for the first Promenade credits the same orchestra. The identification of this file with that track rests on title and length; the Musopen performer page was not opened. Conductor: unknown.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Orchestral performance; Ravel’s 1922 orchestration is the probable version but is not named by any source
fields.note: Neither Commons, the Free Music Archive nor the Internet Archive names the orchestrator. The album’s four Promenades (none between “Samuel Goldenberg and Schmuÿle” and Limoges) match Ravel’s layout, and a 2015 Commons talk-page comment calls the recording Ravel’s orchestration of a rather poor Skidmore performance. The commenter gives no source. Instrument names in the listening notes follow Ravel’s scoring conditionally, as the introduction says; the audio report does not identify instruments.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: No session date is documented. The Internet Archive item says “date unknown, 2008 at the latest”; the Free Music Archive lists the album as released 6 April 2009; this file was uploaded to Commons on 2008-01-21. None of these is a recording date.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: No venue is documented. The Free Music Archive biography describes the orchestra as a semi-professional ensemble of Skidmore students and regional professionals; this is not a recording location.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Mussorgsky’s piano suite (he died in 1881) is public domain; Commons marks the music PD-old-100. An orchestration is a separate work with its own term and is not cleared here.
fields.note: The Commons notice covers Mussorgsky’s music only. If the version is Ravel’s, his orchestration is not assessed in this dossier.

fields.value: Rule 1 — recording release: PD-author public-domain dedication by Musopen, with Wikimedia VRTS permission ticket 2008012110017088.
fields.note: The file description applies PD-author|Musopen to the recording separately from PD-old-100 for the music, and cites the VRTS ticket; the page is in “Items with VRTS permission confirmed”. Musopen’s reproduced policy says the music is public domain with no restrictions; its requests not to sell the recordings and to credit Musopen are courtesy requests, not a non-commercial licence. composer.epithet: He made Russian speech, public crowds and the noises of ordinary life determine the shape of opera.
facts: Piano with Anton Gerke; composition informally with Mily Balakirev; no conservatory education
Guards officer until 1858; civil servant, including work in the Forestry Department
Balakirev, Borodin, Cui and Rimsky-Korsakov; the critic Vladimir Stasov
Operas, dramatic songs and piano music; many works unfinished or published in other composers’ revisions
composer.background:
Mussorgsky grew up on his family’s estate at Karevo, where his mother taught him the piano and his nurse supplied stories that he later associated with his earliest improvisations. The household belonged to the landowning class. The peasant voices he eventually put into songs and operas came from another social world. Sent to Saint Petersburg for schooling, he studied piano with Anton Gerke and entered the School of Guards Cadets in 1852. In 1856 he joined the Preobrazhensky Regiment. His first published piano piece, a polka, belonged to the drawing room.

Meeting Dargomyzhsky and then Balakirev redirected that education. Balakirev taught through playing, criticism and the examination of scores. Mussorgsky left the army in 1858, but composing did not provide a living. The emancipation of the serfs in 1861 disrupted the estate income on which his family depended, and he eventually took civil-service posts. The group later called the Five brought together different professions and musical methods: Borodin was a chemist, Cui a military engineer, Rimsky-Korsakov a naval officer. Their shared opposition to imported academic authority concealed substantial musical disagreements.
